newsitem.title: Austria: ALPINE SKIING-SYKORA EMERGES AS WINNER AFTER SLOW START.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SYKORA EMERGES AS WINNER AFTER SLOW START.

text.p: Two years ago, Thomas Sykora decided it was time to abandon the role of an average ski racer and become a champion.
Few skiers have managed such a transition in more regal style than the 28-year-old Austrian, who has surprised his rivals this winter by becoming a consistent winner.
Sykora has won won five of the eight slaloms staged so far this season and finished second once. He has practically secured the discipline's World Cup title already.
"Two years ago, (Austrian men's coach Werner) Margreiter bluntly told me that if a skier hadn't won a race by the age of 25, then he would never win.
"I just stared at him blankly. Didn't he realise I was already 26 at the time? Or was he just trying to make a point? I didn't argue with him then, but I made sure I proved him wrong," Sykora said.
The turning point in his career came in December 1994, when he was denied a maiden victory at a slalom in Lech, Austria, by Italian Olympic and world champion Alberto Tomba.
"Tomba beat me although he made a major mistake which must have cost him at least a second. At first I was so devastated, I managed no good results for a year.
"Then I just stopped doing safety runs and concentrated only on winning. I raced without making any compromises, just like Tomba," he said. "Then I won Kitzbuehel (in 1996) and everything changed."

Since that breakthrough, Sykora stood on the World Cup slalom podium until the race in Kitzbuehel last weekend -- when he was suffering from hip pains and finished a poor seventh. He improved to fourth in the floodlit slalom in Schladming on Thursday.
The tall and lanky Austrian is now a hot favourite for the world championships, starting on Sunday in Sestriere, although his showing at big events has not been impressive.

"I never had the nerves for big events. A ninth place at the (1993) Morioka world championships was my best result," said Sykora, who failed to complete both the slaloms at the 1994 Lillehammer Olympics and 1996 world championships in Sierra Nevada.
"My goal is to complete two good runs in Sestriere. I like the slope and have always performed well on it. Last year, I was second in (a World Cup race in) Sestriere behind (Austria's Mario) Reiter.
"But I don't need a medal to be a happy person. Maybe I will get a medal because I think this way and am so relaxed," he said.
That Sykora became a sportsman is no surprise as he comes from one of Austria's most famous sports families.

One of his aunts, Maria Sykora, was an 800 metres European athletics championship medallist and former world record holder for the 400 metres hurdles. Another, Elisabeth Prokop, won pentathlon Olympic silver in 1968 and one year later became European pentathlon champion.

Prokop is now the top sports politician in Sykora's native province of Lower Austria. Her husband Gunnar is the country's most successful handball coach, who led the women's team of 'Hypo Suedstadt' to European Cup victory six times.
It was his powerful sports family who arranged for Sykora to have his own private piste in the Hochkar resort, near his hometown of Goestling.
"It's a perfect practice slope, very similar to the (World Cup) slalom piste in Madonna di Campiglo (Italy). I make sure it is always prepared the way I like it -- hard and extremely icy.
"Instead of buying a Porsche, I invested my money in a snow machine (to make artificial snow) and a ski caterpillar," he said. "It's an extreme slope and would be dangerous for the average skier."
Despite the full support of his family, Sykora had a slow start in ski racing and only joined Austria's elite team at the late age of 22.
At 17, Sykora had considered racing for the Netherlands but changed his mind when new International Ski Federation rules required a skier to have the nationality of the country he was starting for.
"At the time, I was very confused about my future, I was too old to become a tennis player -- which had been one of my childhood dreams.
"So instead I trained alone with my father until I was good enough for the Austrian ski team," said Sykora.
When asked to describe his character, the sympathetic Austrian who appears to always have a mischievous grin on his face said: "I'm a cheerful person who always tries to see life from the funny side.
"I don't always deal with life the way an adult should, but I am not a complainer."
